items.title: Understanding consumer vs business confidence
items.description: Latest surveys suggest that Pakistani consumers remain markedly more pessimistic than businesses. A gap between consumers and business sentiment is not unusual, as the two experience and access the economy differently. But if these surveys are credible indicators, the widening divergence warrants closer scrutiny and explanation from policymakers, economists and business leaders. The September State Bank of Pakistan (SBP)–Institute of Business Administration (IBA) Confidence Index stood at 49.1 compared with just 33.6 on the Q3 Ipsos Consumer Confidence Index. This striking gap could reflect differences in how businesses and households interpret headline economic indicators, varying level of trust in government, or, more fundamentally, their contrasting economic realities: a financially stronger minority with greater resources, choices and capacity to absorb shocks versus a much larger population struggling individually with weaker purchasing power and greater vulnerability. Dr Durre Nayab, Director, Socioeconomic Insights and Analytics, and former joint director at the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE), offered a different explanation, attributing the apparent divergence largely to measurement methodology and sampling. “To me, the gap is a measurement artefact. First, the two numbers aren’t on the same scale. The SBP-IBA index is a diffusion index, where 50 signals neutrality, zero indicates no confidence and 100 extreme confidence. The Ipsos index is constructed differently and has historically hovered in the 30s. So, 33.6 cannot be read as ‘16 points below neutral’ in the same way that 49.1 can be described as ‘near neutral’.” Survey results indicate that consumers are less optimistic about Pakistan’s economy than businesses She noted that the direction of the Ipsos index was, in fact, slightly positive: it rose 0.4 points to 33.6, while and 24 per cent of the respondents said the country is heading the right direction, up from 11pc in August 2024. “Second, who gets surveyed matters most,” Ms Nayab said. “The business survey draws from about 2,000 large, Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan-registered firms, with about 500 surveyed each month, selected on the basis of the highest paid-up capital. It, therefore, captures the corporate top tier, not the kiryana store, the mohalla khokha or the small and medium enterprises.” Large firms, she argued, are better positioned to pass higher costs on through prices, benefit from interest rate cuts, and hedge against risks. “Households, meanwhile, absorb those passed-on costs, often on fixed or informal incomes. The two groups are living different economic realities.” Nasim Beg, CEO, Arif Habib Consultancy, believes the contrast stems partly from their different perspectives: businesses tend to be forward-looking, basing decisions on assessment of future economic conditions, while consumers respond more directly to their lived experience. “The average consumer’s behaviour is influenced by lived reality. Over the last five years, Pakistani consumers have suffered a sharp erosion of purchasing power alongside income compression. Even if the economic outlook is improving, households continue to feel the cumulative impact of that squeeze.” Ehsan Malik, former CEO, Pakistan Business Council, also blamed the divergence more to contrasting economic realities than differences in understanding. “Businesses are not truly optimistic: at 49.1, confidence remains below neutral, though expectations are improving. Larger firms can raise prices, alter products, defer investment, hedge risks and lobby for subsidies, guaranteed returns and protection. “Consumers have no such options. They must absorb higher food, electricity, rent and tax costs, while slower inflation does not restore lost purchasing power. “Trust further widens the divide when the burden of adjustment appears unfairly distributed. Consumers understand their vulnerability well. Pakistan has achieved some macroeconomic stabilisation, but confidence will converge only when it translates into secure jobs, recovering real incomes and affordable essentials. “The divergence should therefore be seen as a policy warning, not a survey anomaly or evidence that consumers poorly understand an economy in which spending power has eroded”. Industrialist Majyd Aziz attributed consumers’ pessimism primarily to small paychecks failing to keep pace with rising living costs. Pakistan’s import-dependent economy remains vulnerable to global supply and demand shocks, while deindustrialisation, galloping inflation, and depleting household savings have intensified the squeeze. “Unlike businesses, consumers buy daily and have their feet firmly on the ground,” he said. Mr Aziz also questioned whether the Ipsos Consumer Confidence Index fully captures ground realities, noting that it surveyed 1,000 people by telephone rather than through face-to-face interviews. He found the provincial variations striking: 31pc of respondents in Balochistan believed the country was on the right track, compared to only 14pc in KP. More tellingly, he said, only 10pc of consumers felt comfortable making household purchases, underscoring weak purchasing power and explaining difficulties facing domestic businesses. High electricity, gas, and fuel costs continue to strain household budgets despite the survey showing greater optimism about personal finances. Mr Aziz argued that rising stock prices, property investment, automobile purchases and improving industrial indicators largely reflect the choices available to the affluent and should not automatically be equated with broad-based economic recovery. The survey’s optimism, he said, must, therefore, be weighed against the frustration, uncertainty and vulnerability confronting ordinary consumers. Members of the government’s economic team and the State Bank were approached for comment, but no response had been received by the time this report was filed. The writer is a former Dawn staffer. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, September 28th, 2026

items.title: Aliko Dangote, Nigeria’s truest capitalist? By Suleiman A. Suleiman
items.description: (suleimansuleiman@dailytrust.com; 07066451983 SMS) Nigeria has a complicated relationship with capitalism. For the most part, it is barely understood. In Nigeria, capitalism is often presented as something inherently bad. This draws from the residual legacy of Nigerian Marxism, and a religious ethos that sometimes viewspoverty as a moral trophy. The idea that “money is the root of all evil” remains one of the most popular sayings in our public culture, even though money clearly also does so much good. Nigerians also tend to privilege money above all else, and thus understand capitalism simply as personal accumulation of money. This partly explains why trading, rent-seeking, and briefcase “contracts” remain the predominant forms of ‘business’ activities. Most crucially, we seem to think that the primary purpose of money is to spend it on luxury: mansions, expensive cars, private jets, and anything that elicits that “I pass my neighbour” feeling.Money, not creative labour by which it is generated or preserved, is the most celebrated thing in Nigeria. There are profound consequences for these ambiguous relationship with capitalism, and we suffer them every day in our politics, economy and society, not least an extreme materialism whereby money defines nearly all relationships, and is implicitly or explicitly transacted even wholly ethical contexts like voting, law enforcement, filial relationship, neighbourliness, and even pastoral care by traditional and religious leadership. Moreover, our failure to properly understand capitalism at academic, policy and popular levels has meant an inability to develop anything beyond primitive capitalism. Nigeria has never truly been able to develop a genuinely domestic capitalism on a scale large enough to sustain the world’s sixth most populous country. We have dozens of groceries across nearly every street in every town or city, for example, but not a single Walmart or Sainsbury’s. And similar examples abound across all sectors. This is so in part because we have not thought to institutionalize wealth creation and preservation on a large scale. How many venture-capital companies do we have to invest in start-ups across all sectors? How many patents do we licence per year? How much do we spend collectively on research and development? How many proper business schools do we have here? How many truly large-scale or multi-national companies? Where is Nigeria’s truly serious, realistic and long-term industrial policy? Where is the capacity of the state and government to faithfully implement it? What is the state of our corporate governance, labour and inheritance laws? The list is not exhaustive, off course. But these are the institutions and institutional mechanisms that generate wealth on a large scale and preserve it for the long term. Unfortunately, lacking most of these things, Nigeria remains abjectly poor and unable to preserve wealth for the long term, despite the presence of thousands of “rich people”. When I was growing up in the early 1990s, we heard tales of wealthy families like the Abiolas, the Dantatas, the Maidaribes, the Nzeribes, and so on. Most of these have gone under by now, whereas, elsewhere, some of the wealthiest families 200 years ago remain so today, and the whole society benefits from their wealth in jobs, taxes, the things they produce, and what not. The point is not to romanticise capitalism but to clarify it since a country of 230 million people cannot attain development under our persistent primitive form of capitalism. As I chose to clarify it here, capitalism as is about wealth accumulation through production, and about wealth preservation through institutionalization. The capitalist will get rich, yes, but they would do so by producing something, by creating and preserving value, and by solving problems and meeting the needs of a large enough number of people. We understand money and accumulation in Nigeria, but not enough of production, preservation or institutionalization that are core to a capitalist economy and culture. My argument today, therefore, is that we must bring all these things back in when we think or talk about capitalism in this country. This is what makes Dangote, and what he is trying to do here in Nigeria, important. For me, Dangote represents the closest thing we have to a true capitalist in this sense of wealth accumulation through production. Dangote has been in business since 1977, and his career has followed three phases. He began as a trader, that is, essentially as a middleman between those who produce and those who consume. He then transitioned to the “accumulation through production” phase in the early 2000s as a leading beneficiary of the government’s privatisation programme. With his Dangote Refinery and other business in the Group, he is now effectively not just a producer of things himself, but a builder of big businesses from scratch. According to reports, Dangote was worth $3.3 billion when he first appeared on the Forbes list of richest people in 2008. Today, Bloomberg reports his total worth at $35.5 billion. This means that he is worth more than ten times today than he was in 2008. In other words, he has accumulated more wealth at a shorter pace because he has produced more of the things we all need, from sugar and cement to refined petroleum. How many of those politicians and so-called businessmen who bought off previously state-owned enterprises have been able to turn them around and add value to them, let alone build new large-scale ventures from the start? The point is not to fantasize a single individual, but to hold them up as a model of true capitalism, of wealth accumulation through production, value creation and problem-solving on a large scale. Consider, for example, the Dangote Refinery, the largest of its kind in the world. This project is much more than private capital since it not only adds value to our energy sector, it also has multiplier effects across other sectors and significant impact on our national GDP. Moreover, by giving Nigerians a direct stake in the refinery, it insures against any punitive or rogue governments—and we always have one around the corner in this country—which might seek to derail the entire project for their own selfish ends. Public ownership of the company is a mechanism by which the refinery can be preserved over the longer term. Indeed, even the story of how the refinery was built from scratch to the first gush of refined fuel against all odds right here in Nigeria should itself be case study in our business schools. Future large-scale entrepreneurs could learn something from Dangote’s experience building the refinery from the ground up. And if we are wise, then the Dangote story must be properly documented in biographies, books, and academic articles. These are by themselves important forms of production, value addition, and collective capital for the society as a whole. Finally, is also an entire value system in its own right, and one of its most prized values is the personal discipline of the capitalist. The truest capitalists know that the real value of money, is not conspicuous consumption but for more and more value creation that preserves their own wealth beyond their lifetimes, and also help to lift the entire society along with them. Some of the richest persons of all time belong in this category. In a country where moneybags spend their fortunes on luxury and comfort, Dangote, along with just a few others, is in a class of his own in his personal discipline and frugality. And that too must be documented and passed on. In sum, the capitalist has done his part, and it is left for the state to rise to the occasion by acquiring the capacity needed not only to enforce sound policies and regulations to help preserve capital and wealth, but also for making capitalist enterprise better serve the country at large. The biggest challenge of development in Nigeria has always been how to create a truly capitalist class, to develop and entrench a widespread entrepreneurial culture, and how to shift from a predominantly informal and precapitalist production to capitalist productionon a large scale. In order words Nigeria’s challenge is how to create dozens and dozens of Dangotes right here at home. We now have a living model with which to start. This is the whole point today. The post Aliko Dangote, Nigeria’s truest capitalist? By Suleiman A. Suleiman appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: AI and social catastrophe
items.description: OVER the past 12 months, the capabilities of frontier AI models have remained a central topic of debate. Recent performance demonstrations across a variety of technical fields (maths and bio-genetics in particular) show that scepticism around raw capability at least is a dated position. However, there are still question marks around financial viability, regulation of broad-based societal risks, and impact on workers and labour more generally. The latter two deserve more scrutiny. The first concern, around broad-based risks, has gained quite a bit of attention with a spate of resignations from top AI companies, with departing individuals claiming that AI poses a serious risk to society and carries a non-zero chance of triggering human extinction. What is the pathway of such a catastrophe? The most common position at this point is that, in the absence of clear ethical guardrails, AI tools can be used to create biological weapons of the sort that could trigger large-scale human loss. Others think that, in the wrong/rival hands, AI could be used to trigger weapons of mass destruction. These fears appear to be fairly fantastical, and the timing with which they’re being made public — just when the frontier models are poised for initial public offerings — suggests they’re part of a Silicon Valley hype cycle. However, if these claims about capabilities and the risks they could carry are even remotely true, they pose a much simpler question. If a technology is truly this capable, then what is it even doing in private hands? Historian and economic commentator, Adam Tooze, made an insightful analogy that if we take the claims of societal risk at face value, we’re essentially developing a technology that is similar to the nuclear bomb in the type of catastrophe it can pose, and that too at a much greater scale. The impact of AI on labour markets is something that many workers will face in a variety of ways in the coming years. But the key difference is that the development of the bomb took place through the Manhattan Project, which was entirely governed and steered by the state, with private enterprise playing a junior and often strictly compartmentalised role. AI, on the other hand, is being developed by private enterprise, with private investment steering its priorities, and commercial viability shaping the discourse around it. At any other point in human history, has anything posing purported risks of this nature been allowed to emerge via a process of borderline anarchic market-led competition? The logical corollary of this parallel is that anything that poses large-scale existential risk is too important to be left in private hands. Public regulation determining its development, use, sale/purchase, and evolution becomes a necessity. And that this regulation cannot emerge from the ind­us­­try itself, which is subsumed under intense com­peti­tion and has a vested interest in skirting around various legalities, but rather from the state. Beyond pushback against the fearmongering, there is also some scepticism around AI’s potential to generate astronomic growth in capitalist societies. In particular, Ben Moll and Alex Imas argue in a recent Substack piece that predictions of double-digit AI-driven growth, the kind floated by Dario Amodei, Leopold Aschenbrenner, and various technologists, are unlikely to materialise within the next decade or so, even though making a textbook case for it is relatively simple. Moll and Imas argue that explosive growth is easy to generate in a standard textbook growth model. If automation steadily raises the share of tasks that machines can perform, diminishing returns to capital weaken and eventually disappear once machines can do everything. The core of their position, however, argues that this outcome depends on several assumptions that are unlikely to hold in practice. Automation would need to spread across the whole economy very quickly, not just in cognitive or remote tasks but across physical, messy, and relational work that resists mechanisation. Spending patterns would need to stay proportional even as automated goods become cheap, rather than shifting towards whatever remains scarce, which is the usual pattern of structural change. But a central facet, which these authors don’t give much attention to but others have honed in on, is that in a society where the cost of production approaches zero, there would need to be enough demand to absorb all that cheap, expanded output. Where would such demand come from once automation shifts jobs and income away from wor­kers who spend a large share of what they earn? This brings us back to perhaps the key issue of AI capability that has been drowned out by fears of biological weapons and global catastrophe. The technology’s impact on labour markets is something that many workers will face in a variety of ways in the coming years. It’s not just about a machine replacing a human, though that is the most commonly held view. It’s also about how the threat of a machine replacing humans changes working conditions and the kind of income one can expect to receive. The history of technology adoption in labour processes is often told in large sweeps of history. Technologists tend to use common examples, such as how the arrival of machines after the late 19th century unlocked rapid growth and raised prosperity or how the creation of the ATM didn’t lead to a mass exodus of banking sector jobs. The implication is that society adapts and the outcome is usually positive. What this cheerful story misses out is that adaptation processes produce winners and losers, with the latter taking years to adjust. In a world already characterised by the deskilling of labour, people rendered jobless by a machine (or the threat of a machine) won’t suddenly find alternative employment. Those two or three decades in which the labour market sorts itself out will seem minuscule in a broad sweep of history, but for those living through this period, it will be a particularly bleak eternity. The writer teaches sociology at Lums. X: @umairjav Published in Dawn, September 28th, 2026

items.title: NAFCO builds GH¢100m food buffer as Ghana moves to strengthen food security
items.description: The National Food Buffer Stock Company (NAFCO) has revamped its National Food Reserve Programme with an initial GH¢100 million government funding to strengthen Ghana’s ability to respond to food crises and price pressures. The programme was introduced in response to reported gluts of grains, particularly rice and maize, in some parts of the country. According to NAFCO Chief Executive Officer, George Abradu-Otoo, the company had, by December 31, 2025, stocked 36,597 bags of maize, 21,287 bags of rice and 5,982 bags of gari in warehouses across Tamale, Badu, Kumbungu, Dzodze, Wenchi and Kumasi. “Under this program, NAFCO is required to keep or hold some quantity of food as a buffer for the nation and release it when necessary, including emergencies, disasters and high food cost seasons,” he said. He said the programme would help keep inflation in check, reduce post-harvest losses and support government interventions in agriculture. The development forms part of broader measures by NAFCO to strengthen Ghana’s food security architecture, including the rehabilitation and expansion of storage facilities across the country. Abradu-Otoo said many of the company’s warehouses had deteriorated and become unfit for purpose. NAFCO has therefore commenced an aggressive programme to rehabilitate and expand its storage facilities, with support from the Ministry of Food and Agriculture, ECOWAS and the World Food Programme. The programme also includes the provision of laboratories, testing equipment, tracking and digital devices, as well as training and retraining of personnel. NAFCO’s regional operations have also been strengthened, with all 16 regional offices now operational. The CEO said the company’s 2025 performance marked a major turnaround. NAFCO recorded a net profit before tax of GH¢91.7 million, its highest since its establishment, after posting a GH¢19.4 million loss the previous year. The company also paid GH¢20.3 million in taxes to the state in 2025, the highest annual tax contribution in its 16-year history. Abradu-Otoo attributed the turnaround partly to structural reforms, including the establishment of a dedicated Procurement Department, a strengthened Internal Audit Department, a fortified Food Safety Department and the reconstitution of the Board and its sub-committees. He said the company also improved payments to suppliers and resourced its regional offices. “The year 2025 was a turning point. We recorded our highest profit in 16 years. We improved payments to our suppliers. We resourced our regions. We paid the highest tax to the state,” he said. “We have consolidated. We have shown what is possible. Now we build.”

items.title: El edadismo cambia el discurso: de las antiarrugas a la longevidad
items.description: Hay algo deprimente en las bellezas de Hollywood. La mayoría siguen siendo guapas, con estiramientos faciales y una determinación desesperada, hasta que se marchitan. Gloria Swanson no. Parte del atractivo de esta dama reside en que ha evolucionado hacia la madurez”, alababa la escritora Helena Huntington Smith en un perfil de Swanson publicado en 1930. La actriz estaba a punto de cumplir 31 años, así que encaraba el ocaso de su carrera, pero a diferencia de las mujeres que habían luchado de forma evidente contra el paso del tiempo, a ella no se le notaba. Ella estaba envejeciendo bien, frente a otras que lo hacían mal. Seguir leyendo

items.title: The anmol ‘crack’ down on Queen Pinky
items.description: On the morning of April 7, Karachi’s Baghdadi police were alerted to a body on a footpath near a school in Lyari. Brown shirt, checked trousers, about 25 years old, no ID. Of note was a small tin sealed in golden foil that was found on his person. It said: “Queen Medam Pinky 🖤Don 🖤Naam hi kafi hai. Enjoy.” The Baghdadi police put the body down as Unidentified Drug Addict in the roznamcha and dispatched it to a morgue. On May 9, they registered a murder case and nominated the name on the tin: Pinky. A forensic toxicology report confirmed their suspicion a few days later that it had traces of the A-class Schedule I narcotic cocaine. On May 12, Pinky was declared arrested. In the official telling, Pinky was taken into custody from a flat in Karachi’s Garden on May 12 by the Sindh Police and a federal intelligence agency. Her arrest, it emerged, according to one version of events, was based on a tip-off. Pinky’s ex-husband had snitched on her to a sub-inspector in Karachi to tell him where she was hiding. The policeman, who cannot be named due to his current deputation, was ecstatic—he had been on Pinky’s case since 2019 and had once even come close. She had been dodging arrest for eight years and was thus well known to the Lahore and Karachi police, Counter-Terrorism Department and Anti-Narcotics Force as a most-wanted criminal in 28 cases involving narcotics, illegal arms and violent crimes. The joint operation team said it found in her flat boxes of packaging material, sealed tins like the one found on the Unidentified Drug Addict, other drugs, and a 9mm pistol with ten rounds. But most importantly, it had about 1.5kg of cocaine, which is worth as much as Rs30 million—a single seizure that equaled what the police intercepted from the entire City district in the first eight months of the year. When Medam Pinky was presented at the Judicial Complex inside Central Prison Karachi on May 17, she challenged this version of the arrest loud and clear. As she was dragged into a police van—restrained by a clutch of women police officers who struggled to cover her face with a white chador—she shouted. “These people picked me up from Lahore and brought me here 22 days ago!” The reporters latched onto this but she theatrically parried their questions: “ Hum to doobay hain sanam, in sab ko lai doobay gain .” I may be drowning, my love, but I will take all of them down with me too. At one point in the ensuing media circus, a PDF list of 326 Karachi-based telephone numbers, supposedly from her smartphone, was reported as leaked. This news sent shivers down the city’s most expensive spines. The personal information doxxing was devastating for businessmen, journalists, bankers, and industrialists, whose CNICs and home and work addresses were spilled all over the internet. Frantic calls were made and eventually word had to be put out that the list was fake. By this time, Pinky had captured the nation’s imagination. Television news channels were tickled pink that they could safely use the title “Queenpin” to salt the storytelling. TikTok—unencumbered by journalistic decorum—hashtagged her as #CocaineQueen . Indeed, the entire country had something to say about her brazen appearances. Look at the way she saunters in. Imagine coming to court in pajamas and a T-shirt! What’s with the vintage sunglasses? Shouldn’t she be in handcuffs? Bulk supply The officer who had received the tip-off accompanied the intelligence agency to the centre of Pinky’s web, Lahore. This is where over half of her contacts, 785 out of 1,286, resided. The Punjab capital, along with Islamabad and Rawalpindi, is a hot market for cocaine. A former investigation officer at the Anti-Narcotics Force explained that most of it is snuck in by air, usually as capsules swallowed by mules, a majority of whom travel from Africa. Others arrive from Europe carrying smaller quantities concealed among ordinary belongings such as infant formula. Large consignments arrive by sea. Commercial vessels are used as unwitting vehicles. The packages of narcotics are concealed either inside a container in its cargo or within the structure of the container itself, hidden in the walls or below the floor. Reefer containers are used for their refrigeration units. Pinky’s supplier was a Nigerian, identified as Chike Ochuba Chinwuba, according to her case file available with Dawn . The cocaine first came to Sialkot and then made its way to Lahore. Once it arrived, it had to be bulked up. Pinky could turn 1.5kg from abroad into 5kg by adding impurities. She told the police that “Google Uncle” taught her how to mix with ketamine, methamphetamine, ephedrine, and lidocaine as they mimic cocaine’s sensory effects, or alter the perceived potency. “Pure cocaine is rare here,” said the former ANF official. That is why most of what you get in Karachi is synthetically created in homes and labs. “And [the mixing] has resulted in deaths.” Smooth operator Selling the cocaine was fairly straightforward after Pinky’s brother Nasir helped her mix and package it. All orders were placed directly with medam who would only entertain customers with a reference. Communication took place entirely over WhatsApp messages and voice notes. Pinky would share the bank account of an “accountant” and after a screenshot confirmed the payment, she shared the customer’s location with the rider and dispatched the delivery. Medam Pinky's Karachi Medam Pinky's Karachi A geographic breakdown of the addresses found on Pinky's client list. Hover or tap a district to focus. Client density Low High Street network: OpenStreetMap contributors, via Wikimedia Commons ("Karachi Pakistan street map.svg"), recoloured & composited — district boundaries are illustrative, not surveyed. Hatched areas are cantonments and sit outside the seven client districts. "> Deliveries to Karachi were organised through people she hired, mostly women, who travelled there by bus, with the cocaine concealed in small packages in their clothes and luggage. Bus staff helped couriers conceal the drugs under the seats or inside luggage compartments. Altogether, one kilogramme was dispatched a week. Pinky’s other brother Shaukat would be waiting in Karachi to receive the packages, which he would measure off, put into the tins, brand and distribute among three handlers, who delivered them by riders. Everyone reported to Shaukat. None of the payments was made directly to Pinky as she had two finance handlers, Sohail and Zeeshan, whose bank accounts were used. Muhammad Sameer managed ATM and other online transactions through four different banks. In one account, transactions over a year and a half amounted to Rs29.46 million. Across the four accounts—under the names of Sohail, Zeeshan and Sameer—she had Rs32.7 million. Customer satisfaction Cocaine is an elite drug because of who can afford to keep using it. It’s the people with the house with a garage and an eight-million-rupee car parked in the driveway. That is the point, said Ustad, a user-turned-police informer. Age isn’t a consideration. Customers range from 14 to 65 years. At a party, the customer reviews are glowing. “Her stuff is good, not gonna lie,” said Inaya*. The first time she had tried the white stuff, she felt like she was “on top of the world”. Another client, Hadi*, a 32-year-old introvert, experienced a personality transplant—the shyness that had plagued him his whole life simply switched off. “He was flirting left, right, and centre. He was unstoppable, man,” said his best friend, as they described the experience snorting cocaine. They had come to know Pinky on a desperate night. “I was wasted…but had to walk back home,” said Hadi, who lived two streets from the house where they had been partying. “A friend suggested cocaine. A line.” At 4am, the tin, bearing Pinky’s tagline, was delivered to their doorstep. The effect doesn’t last, though. Fifteen minutes, stretch it to 20, and the floor drops out from under the high as fast as it had arrived. You chase that first quarter of an hour for the rest of the night and pay for it in thousand-rupee increments, said Hadi*. “There goes your money,” added Inaya*. Package deal Pinky’s delivery network may have been pulling in the clients, but it was also putting her on the police radar. The sub-inspector who would go on to arrest her seven years later, first came across her name in 2019, while he was posted to DHA, Karachi and told to look into the area’s drug problem. All he had back then was the nickname and a number. So they pulled the call detail record and ran the most frequent numbers through TrueCaller. Then they picked one number that barely showed up. “ Sab se gareeb admi ,” the SI told Dawn . That would have been the poorest customer. They called him and said a complaint had been filed. In exchange for immunity, he agreed to score 2g of cocaine for the cops. After two days of dillydallying, the delivery was finally made. A man and woman showed up on a motorcycle, both of whom were pulled in. But their lips were sealed and eventually they had to be released. It was the second time round that the rider sang. His shift ran from 8pm to 2am for Rs70,000 a month. A single packet weighed 12g, worth about Rs300,000. At the time he was caught, he had already sold four. The police told him to keep working and shadowed him on their motorcycles. The next pickup point was Gulshan-e-Iqbal, but 15 minutes later, it was changed to a french fries kiosk in Landhi. A man and woman came on a motorcycle again. This time, though, the man was none other than Shaukat. That’s when Pinky entered the picture. “She tried to negotiate her brother’s release,” the sub-inspector said. “Her final offer was Rs900,000 with the condition: brother first, then the money.” The police declined and locked Shaukat up, but he would be out soon enough. After that, “Pinky had figured out the tricks of the trade,” said the sub-inspector. Her riders multiplied and the drop points evolved. The tins were no longer handed over in person but tucked under a dustbin inside an ATM. While the chase for Pinky finally ended this year, her name had already acquired a life of its own. Despite the media blitz, and the effort it took to nab her the police official insisted Pinky was not the drug tycoon she had been made out to be. “She was a mid-level player, no kingpin,” he said. “She was living normally, like you and me…she didn’t have a big house or scary dogs.” He believed her reputation had grown faster than her operation. The business was not unlike any other: word spread about the quality of the product, customers returned, and the brand name acquired a currency of its own. But where was that name from? Claim to fame Pinky was born Anmol in Gwadar in 1995 and was raised in Karachi. She dropped out of school in the eighth grade and set off to Lahore with dreams of becoming an actress. Several failed auditions later, she met Rana Nasir and eventually married him. Soon, she began transporting drugs for him, and ultimately climbed the ladder to become his manager. They divorced 10 years later. For Anmol, a decade was all she needed to reroute Nasir’s clients. All of them knew one name: Pinky. It was a name she had chosen as a teenager, one for the world of modelling and elite parties. “The name has glamour,” the police officer said. “If it was Gulbano, Nuzhat or Fatima, people would not be as interested. [Pinky] is not easily forgettable.” Even after she moved to Lahore, her customers continued to find her. The truth is that there are players far grander than Pinky, who operate quietly, produce more but rarely become the story themselves. Pinky did the opposite. Her name did the rest. *Names have been changed to protect privacy.

items.title: La rabia de los jóvenes por la vivienda activa la cuenta atrás en el reloj de Sol: 48 horas para un decreto real
items.description: La rabia acumulada en España desde hace unos años por la permanente crisis de acceso a la vivienda, sobre todo entre los más jóvenes, ha tomado el centro de Madrid. Miles de ellos que siguieron la semana pasada por televisión el desahucio de una mujer de 87 años a manos de una empresa de inversión se manifestaron por las calles del centro de la ciudad y, al acabar, muchos desplegaron sus tiendas de campaña en la Puerta del Sol. De ahí no se van a mover, como los que abanderaron el 15-M hace 15 años. A la mañana siguiente, el domingo, quedó claro que habían logrado crear una pequeña república, con sus políticas y lógicas internas, para canalizar sus frustraciones. La sensación de que el mundo no es inamovible y se puede cambiar lo invadió todo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: De la Corrala Utopía a Maricarmen: la eterna discordia por la vivienda en la izquierda
items.description: En mitad de un mensaje centrado en celebrar el acuerdo presupuestario para 2023, Ione Belarra pegó un volantazo y cambió el titular. Endureciendo el gesto, la líder de Podemos y entonces ministra de Derechos Sociales denunció la “resistencia total” del PSOE a aprobar la ley de vivienda. A continuación, reclamó a la gente movilizarse contra los socialistas. No se ve algo así con frecuencia: un miembro del Gobierno llamando a manifestarse contra su socio en ese Gobierno. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Maricarmen, una marca internacional que inspira a 20 asociaciones europeas por una vivienda digna: “Esto trasciende fronteras”
items.description: Vinieron a Madrid para contraprogramar una de las ferias inmobiliarias más importantes de Europa , The District. Y se encontraron con una mujer de 87 años que iba a ser ―y fue, ante sus ojos― desahuciada . Unos 200 activistas por la vivienda de más de 20 países del continente decidieron entonces sumarse, primero, a las manifestaciones contra el desalojo y, después, a la acampada frente a la sede del Gobierno madrileño, en la Puerta del Sol. Personas de Irlanda, Alemania, Portugal, Francia, Inglaterra, Grecia, Rumanía o Suiza, entre otros, que ven en el caso de Maricarmen un punto de inflexión y esperan que el movimiento español se extienda por ciudades de todo el mundo, incluidas las suyas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Es el mismo 15-M
items.description: Han pasado 15 años: el tiempo que Ortega dijo que duran las generaciones. En 2011, las tiendas de campaña se instalaron en la Puerta del Sol y los chicos se vistieron —entonces habríamos dicho “nos vestimos”— con unas camisetas en las que se leía “juventud sin futuro”. Ya en aquel tiempo la vivienda se convirtió en una preocupación social, y aquella indignación abrió la puerta a un ciclo político que casi todo el mundo había dado por zanjado. Ahora la acampada ha regresado. Pero la rabia y el descontento con un sistema que incumple el pacto social no han vuelto. Sencillamente, nunca se fueron. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ortega Smith reprochó a una subordinada “falta de interés” durante su baja maternal: “No has venido a un solo pleno, no has venido a nada”
items.description: El Tribunal Supremo ha rechazado la querella por trato vejatorio y degradante interpuesta por una empleada de Vox contra el exportavoz del partido en el Ayuntamiento de Madrid Javier Ortega Smith, a la que este cesó como directora de Comunicación del grupo municipal el mismo día en que se reincorporaba tras una baja por maternidad. El auto del Supremo, fechado el pasado día 17, del que ha sido ponente la magistrada Susana Polo, considera que los hechos no revisten gravedad suficiente para constituir un delito contra la integridad moral de la querellante, pero tacha la conducta de Ortega Smith de “impropia”, sus palabras de “desafortunadas e improcedentes”, indicativas “incluso de una posible discriminación indirecta por razón de sexo” y le reprocha “un comportamiento un tanto machista que se pone de relieve por parte de la querellante”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El delegado en Ceuta solicitó al Gobierno refuerzos ante el agravamiento de la presión migratoria una semana antes de la avalancha
items.description: El delegado del Gobierno en Ceuta, Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, envió una propuesta al Ministerio del Interior una semana después de la publicación de la sentencia del Tribunal Supremo, que prohibía las devoluciones en caliente de inmigrantes que entraran a nado , para que se reformara la Ley de Extranjería. Para ese día, 16 de julio, habían intentado entrar más de 700 personas a nado desde Marruecos y lo habían logrado 52. Más tarde, el 24, seis días antes de que cruzaran la frontera unas 80.000 personas, remitió otra comunicación dirigida al Ministerio de Política Territorial solicitando medidas de refuerzo y la creación de un centro de triaje porque la presión migratoria era ya grave, según confirman a EL PAÍS distintas fuentes que conocieron estos intercambios. Para ese momento habían intentado entrar más de 1.300 personas y 172 lo habían conseguido. Fuentes del Ejecutivo y de Interior explican que se atendió a los requerimientos y se dotó de refuerzos policiales antes de la avalancha del 30 de julio. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La Flaca sigue buscando a su padre bajo los escombros de La Guaira
items.description: El camino hasta las torres obliga a cubrirse la nariz. Ya no huele a cadáver, como en los primeros días, pero la tierra en suspensión de cientos de toneladas de cemento molido se clava en la garganta y los lagrimales. El sol empieza a ceder y es entonces cuando llegan los zancudos, en manada, a morder la piel sudada y sucia. Los picos continúan golpeando el cemento tres meses después y los pitidos de las excavadoras dando marcha atrás son insoportables cuando suenan todos a la vez. La gente ya no grita de dolor. Como mucho, se oyen órdenes de un militar y alguien que alerta de que ha encontrado una calavera, inalcanzable todavía entre dos placas de concreto. Y ahí, en lo alto de una torre partida en dos, a la altura del sexto piso, con el cielo rosa al fondo, surge una figura que parece una gacela, con su celular siempre en la mano. Es Wallesca Pérez, de 23 años, a la que todos en esa esquina llaman La Flaca. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Bernardo Atxaga, entre golondrinas y demonios: “A veces el humor cruel desvela una realidad”
items.description: Solemos pensar que la tumba es ese lugar donde nuestros restos pasarán el resto de la eternidad. Pero no es así. En ello reparó el escritor Bernardo Atxaga (Asteasu, 75 años) paseando por Zestoa, Gipuzkoa, el pueblo del legendario boxeador Urtain : “Llegamos a un cementerio y le pregunté a un vecino que iba en un tractor si sabía dónde estaba enterrado Urtain. Resulta que habían sido compañeros de colegio, qué casualidad, y me dijo que aquel era el cementerio, pero que habían retirado los restos a los 25 años del entierro”. Esa información tocó ese disparador que tiene Atxaga en la cabeza y que pone en marcha sus novelas. Y de ahí salieron los demonios y las golondrinas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El ‘true crime’ de Chiquito de la Calzada
items.description: El capo de programas de Antena 3 no quería a Chiquito de la Calzada en Genio y figura. Fue el empeño personal de Tomás Summers lo que hizo que Chiquito llegase a nuestras vidas. Las palabras textuales del gerifalte fueron “quitadme a ese señor mayor del programa”. Summers se plantó y dijo que sin ese señor no habría programa en septiembre. Este fue el germen de un caso extraordinario en la historia de la cultura popular española. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El nuevo hito de Kenny Ruiz: primer español en el manga japonés y, ahora, en crear una historia de ‘Star Wars’
items.description: El hermano menor imaginaba y pedía. El mayor escuchaba y, durante un tiempo, ejecutó. “Le contaba cualquier milonga, y me la dibujaba. Yo quería sobre todo historias, el diseño era el medio”, relata Kenny Ruiz (Alicante, 45 años). Cree recordar que tendría ocho años cuando abrumaba con sus ocurrencias al pobre Raúl, que entraba en la adolescencia. Y que, un día, se cansó. “Hazlo tú”, le contestó de golpe. Y añadió: “Hazlo mal, lo importante es que esté hecho. Ya estará bien”. Ahora que hasta tiene alumnos, Kenny les repite aquella enseñanza. Y aunque sigue sin considerarse un “virtuoso” como su hermano mayor, hoy conocido como el grafitero El niño de las pinturas, tan mal no lo hizo. Ha publicado todo tipo de cómics ―europeo, estadounidense, japonés― y luce un hito imbatible: suyo fue el estreno de un occidental como autor de mangas para el mercado nipón . Varios años después, acaba de actualizar su lista de hazañas: La senda del sable de luz (Planeta Cómic) es la primera historia oficial de Star Wars concebida y realizada enteramente por un español. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Inteligencia artificial, pan y circo
items.description: Vivimos tiempos extraordinarios en los que un trabajador de una tecnológica abandona el barco soltando una barbaridad sin ninguna evidencia y no solo se hace ultraviral, sino que medios de comunicación de todo el globo le dan crédito sin cuestionar sus argumentos. Quien no haya estado en una cueva sabrá que me refiero a ese joven exempleado de Anthropic, que el pasado día 9 se despidió espetando que los desarrolladores de la inteligencia artificial (IA) creen que podría matarnos a todos antes de que termine la década. Ese mismo día, su ya exjefe le puso cifras: más de un 10% de probabilidades. Al día siguiente, Anthropic alertó de posibles intentos de usar su IA generativa para crear armas biológicas. El día 12, su fundador, Dario Amodei, mostró su temor a una IA tan inteligente que perdamos el control y se apodere de internet, y pidió ralentizar —que no frenar— su desarrollo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: François Hollande: “Europa se enfrenta a una crisis existencial”
items.description: El despacho, en un cuarto piso de la calle de Rivoli de París, tiene unas vistas impresionantes a los jardines de las Tullerías. En la entrada del amplio apartamento, un póster de la primera campaña de François Mitterrand parece una profecía: “El candidato de los republicanos”. Una unión parecida a la que busca ahora desde la retaguardia el hombre que abre la puerta y saluda a los periodistas con un traje negro. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La crisis energética aboca a los gobiernos a tomar más medidas a las puertas de un superaño electoral en Europa
items.description: Tiene algo de déjà vu , de día de la marmota: cuatro años después de la brutal crisis energética provocada por Vladímir Putin , Europa vuelve a estar en las mismas. Los chalecos amarillos han anunciado su regreso a las carreteras francesas el 17 de octubre, con el precio de la gasolina —y sobre todo del diésel— como catalizador. En Portugal se suceden los bocinazos y las marchas lentas de automóviles . E Irlanda, con nuevas protestas en el horizonte, no termina de cerrar el estallido de la pasada primavera , cuando los manifestantes llegaron a bloquear el acceso a la única refinería del país. Todo incipiente, muy incipiente, pero indicativo de un descontento que está lejos de amainar. Una olla a presión de final incierto y que obliga a los Gobiernos a tomar medidas urgentes. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Las izquierdas, en vilo hasta calibrar la hondura del descontento social
items.description: En lo inmediato, el Gobierno tiene que dar una primera respuesta sobre la vivienda a sus socios de izquierda y a la calle. Por eso, negocia “contrarreloj”, según expresión de su presidente, Pedro Sánchez, con los grupos parlamentarios que forman la coalición, pero también con Junts , cuyos planteamientos se alejan de la intervención de los poderes públicos. El Real Decreto-ley, ya bautizado “decreto Maricarmen”, puede ver la luz en el Consejo de Ministros de este martes y evitar durante un mes desahucios y el aumento de los alquileres, pero decaerá, como ocurrió hace seis meses, si en ese tiempo el Congreso no lo convalida . Seguir leyendo

items.title: España afronta desde Rumania la lucha de la OTAN contra los ataques de drones: “El sistema debe repensarse y actualizarse”
items.description: Cuando los megáfonos de la base aérea 57 Mihail Kogalniceanu en Rumania comenzaron a escupir a las 3.45 de la madrugada por los altavoces “alpha scramble, alpha scramble”, los siete militares españoles de guardia salieron de la cama medio adormilados, pero con la idea clara de lo que tenían que hacer: armarse, despegar dos aviones F-18 en menos de 15 minutos y dirigirse a la frontera con Ucrania para neutralizar una posible amenaza aérea. El objetivo, un dron ruso que había traspasado a territorio aliado, fue finalmente derribado hacia las cinco de la madrugada. Ese 16 de agosto era la primera vez que la OTAN eliminaba uno de estos dispositivos y lo hizo gracias a un piloto español de 27 años. “Es un motivo de orgullo, sin duda”, dice con rostro serio el teniente coronel Alberto Borja Calvo, jefe del destacamento que el Ejército del Aire y del Espacio español mantiene en la misión de la Policía Aérea Reforzada de la OTAN en Rumania . Seguir leyendo

items.title: José Ignacio Goirigolzarri: “El contrato social premia a los mayores y perjudica a los jóvenes”
items.description: A mediados de los duros años ochenta, cuando la heroína diezmaba a la juventud de los barrios, el general y exministro Manuel Gutiérrez Mellado promovía la Fundación de Ayuda contra la Drogadicción (FAD) para enfrentarse a la plaga. Por aquel entonces José Ignacio Goirigolzarri avanzaba en una exitosa carrera en el Banco de Bilbao que lo llevaría después a los puestos más altos del sector: consejero delegado de BBVA y presidente de Bankia (tras el rescate) y de CaixaBank. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Todo lo que falló antes del asesinato de Diana
items.description: El 14 de septiembre de 2024, tres meses antes de ser asesinada, Diana Marisol Vázquez Rojas, de 29 años, nacida en una remota región de Paraguay y sin residencia legal en en España desde que aterrizara en Madrid el 19 de Mayo de 2022, se armó de valor y se presentó en la comisaría de policía de Usera, justo a la vuelta de su casa. “Pido la orden de protección sabiendo que a él le conocen y le respetan porque siempre va armado, y no le tiembla la mano para hacer lo que sea. Temo por mi vida y por la de las personas que me quieran ayudar”, escribió de su puño y letra tras su denuncia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El alcalde de Puertollano es imputado por acoso laboral

items.title: Ser clarito
items.description: Rosa Montero ha escrito una estupenda novela de acción, Un día en la vida de Clarita (Alfaguara, 2026). En sus páginas saltan de un sitio para otro los riesgos, las aventuras y las situaciones difíciles. No conviene dar detalles del argumento, porque se trata de una novela corta, vertiginosa, y la autora pide en el epílogo que tengamos mucho cuidado en las reseñas y las conversaciones entre amigos. Si contamos algunos sucesos, si adelantamos el desenlace, puede destriparse el juego de sorpresas narrativas que sostiene la obra. Así que no voy a mencionar los elementos que comparte con las novelas policiacas, las hazañas de los héroes y las historias de piratas que navegan entre el miedo, las intuiciones de naufragio y los abordajes. No hablo de pistolas, atracadores, cajas de banco y sospechosos. Pero sí hablo de un elemento importante: la persona. Porque hasta la persona más callada es todo un elemento. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Facts first
items.description: WORLD News Day comes at a difficult moment for journalism. Never has so much information been available so quickly, and never has it been so easy for propaganda, lies, manipulated imagery and AI-generated material to circulate alongside fact. The challenge is no longer simply access to information, but knowing what deserves belief. This year’s message, ‘Choose trusted journalism’, is therefore particularly apt. Yet trust cannot be demanded by news organisations as a birthright. It must be earned through the daily, often invisible work of checking claims, verifying evidence, consulting multiple sources, separating fact from opinion and correcting mistakes openly. In a media environment that rewards speed, outrage and certainty, such principles may appear old-fashioned. They are, in fact, journalism’s strongest defence. They also remain essential because false information can inflame tensions and erode confidence in institutions. Newsrooms must look inward. Every sensational headline, careless error or blurring of reporting and commentary weakens public confidence and makes serious journalism harder to distinguish from the flood of material surrounding it. But responsibility does not rest with journalists alone. In Pakistan, the work of verification is made more difficult by pressures on reporters and news organisations, restricted access, interruptions to communications and the use of legal and administrative measures that inhibit independent reporting. When journalists cannot investigate freely, citizens know less about the exercise of power. When communications are blocked during moments of crisis or political tension, rumour gains ground. This is why press freedom and public access to credible information are inseparable. A society cannot demand trustworthy journalism while simultaneously making the practice of it more precarious. That is why World News Day should be less a celebration of the press than a reminder of mutual obligations. Journalists owe the public accuracy, fairness, independence and the humility to correct themselves. Governments owe journalists the freedom to ask difficult questions, pursue uncomfortable facts and publish without intimidation. Readers, too, must learn to recognise the difference between reporting built on evidence and content engineered for reaction. News organisations can help by being more transparent about how stories are sourced, verified and corrected, and by resisting pressures that reward sensationalism over substance. The problem of misinformation will not be solved by adding yet more information to an already crowded stream. What matters is whether information has been questioned, corroborated and placed in context. In an age when technology can create convincing falsehoods in seconds, scrutiny is not an optional extra. It is the value journalism must continue to provide — and the reason it must continue to be protected. Published in Dawn, September 28th, 2026

items.title: Oil heads higher as US-Iran peace talks in stalemate
items.description: Oil prices rebounded more than 1% on ‌Monday after US President Donald Trump rejected a peace deal from Iran to resolve their conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, keeping tensions in the Middle East elevated. Brent crude futures rose $1.32, or 1.27%, to $105.64 a barrel by ​0036 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $93.11 a barrel, up 70 ​cents, or 0.76%. Iran announced a peace proposal last week at the UN ⁠General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari ​mediators. Trump said on Saturday he rejected the plan, but told Axios in a phone ​interview on Sunday that he expected US negotiators to engage in more talks this week. “Geopolitical risks remain elevated, as the Houthis and Iran continued their attacks on Saudi Arabia, leaving regional supply flows vulnerable,” ANZ ​analysts said in a note. Yemen’s Saudi-led coalition said early on Saturday it had intercepted two ballistic ​missiles and two drones launched by the Iran-backed Houthis towards the kingdom. Brent edged up 0.4% last week but ‌WTI ⁠lost 7.9% on concerns that the US may ban diesel exports to ease record prices which could curb US refining output. “Refined oil products remain a pressure point, with record US diesel prices intensifying inflation risks and prompting renewed debate over potential export curbs,” ANZ analysts said. Any restriction ​on US diesel exports ​would tighten supply outside ⁠the US, with European prices reacting to the prospect of reduced American supply, they added. Meanwhile, crude oil exports from key Middle East producers rebounded ​in September to 12.8 million barrels per day, the highest since ​the war ⁠started in February, preliminary data from Kpler showed on Monday, as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates boosted exports. The rebound came following a recovery in shipments via the Strait of Hormuz, ⁠which were ​set to hit about 7.4 million bpd this month, ​the data showed, as Saudi Arabia diverted exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu to its eastern Ras ​Tanura port following attacks that damaged its East-West pipeline.

items.title: GAF sets Sept. 28–30 for Documentation, Body Selection Exercise
items.description: The Ghana Armed Forces (GAF) has announced a three-day Documentation and Body Selection Exercise for qualified applicants who applied under its 2026/2027 Enlistment Exercise. The exercise is scheduled to run from September 28 to 30, 2026 , following the closure of the online application process on September 23. The exercise will be conducted at designated centres in the Northern and Southern sectors. The GAF said applicants who have successfully qualified for this stage will receive text messages containing details of their assigned centres, reporting dates and other instructions. Those who receive the notifications are required to report to their designated centres on the specified dates and comply with all instructions issued by the Armed Forces. For applicants in the Northern Sector , the exercise will take place at the 4 Infantry Battalion, Uaddara Barracks, Kumasi . Applicants in the Southern Sector are to report to the Nicholson Stadium at the Air Force Base in Accra . The Documentation and Body Selection Exercise marks the next major stage in the 2026/2027 recruitment process after the completion of online applications. The exercise is expected to allow the Armed Forces to document and physically assess applicants who have progressed to this stage of the enlistment process. The GAF has therefore urged qualified applicants to pay close attention to the information contained in the text messages sent to them. Applicants are also expected to take note of their assigned centres, reporting dates and all instructions communicated by the Armed Forces. The exercise forms part of the GAF’s ongoing process to select eligible candidates for the 2026/2027 Enlistment Exercise.

items.title: PTI dares govt to impose governor’s rule in KP
items.description: • Panjutha warns move would further deteriorate situation in province; Shahid Khattak proposes assembly resignations, street protests • KP speaker asks police chief to provide details of arrested, detained MPAs ISLAMABAD/PESHAWAR: Amid rising demand in the Centre for the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, senior PTI leader Naeem Haider Panjutha has challenged the federal government to go ahead with the move, warning that it would further deteriorate the situation in the province. “You have already stolen the people’s mandate, stripped them of their two-thirds majority and reserved seats, filed thousands of politically motivated cases, imprisoned tens of thousands, including Imran Khan, raided homes, violated the sanctity of chadar and chardiwari, and imprisoned women, including Bushra Bibi and Imran Khan’s sisters,” Advocate Naeem Haider Panjutha said while talking to Dawn. He said the government should try imposing governor’s rule. “You have no idea what the people of KP are capable of. They will rise up and sweep your governor’s rule away,” he added. Replying to a question, Mr Panjutha said PTI would never retreat from its struggle for Haqeeqi Azadi (true freedom). “Our movement will continue until constitutional supremacy and the rule of law are restored, all political prisoners, including Imran Khan, are released, and the people’s mandate is respected,” he said. “Our struggle will not end until Pakistan stands upon the principles of justice, equality and accountability embodied in the vision of Riyasat-i-Madina,” he added. He claimed that no threats, emergency, governor’s rule or political repression could break PTI’s resolve, and that its struggle for freedom could not be silenced. “Haqeeqi Azadi is our destination, constitutional supremacy is our demand, and our struggle will continue until justice prevails,” Mr Panjutha said. PTI’s parliamentary leader, Shahid Khattak, has also questioned the purpose of remaining in a parliament that, he said, could not even protect the dignity and security of its own MNAs. “What is the point of sitting in a parliament that cannot even protect the dignity and security of its own MNAs?” he said. “My proposal is that we resign from the assemblies and take our struggle to the streets. We are not afraid of arrest. We are not afraid of bullets, guns or any form of pressure. We are soldiers of Imran Khan. A public rally will take place under all circumstances, and we will not turn back until Imran Khan is released, political prisoners are freed, this failed system is replaced, and the supremacy of the Constitution and the rule of law are restored,” he stated. KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi while talking to the media in Peshawar on September 25 disclosed that consultations were held over the possibility of governor’s rule in the province ahead of PTI’s protest march , which was scheduled for September 27 but was later postponed to October 4. Details of arrested MPAs Meanwhile, KP Speaker Babar Saleem Swati on Sunday sought details from the provincial police chief about lawmakers who had been arrested or detained. The details were sought in a letter addressed to KP Inspector General of Police Zulfiqar Hameed, a copy of which is available with Dawn. The speaker sought the information under Articles 66 and 67, read with Article 127, of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, the Provincial Assembly of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Procedure and Conduct of Business Rules, 2025, and the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Provincial Assembly (Powers, Immunities and Privileges) Act, 2026. Mr Swati informed the police chief that, being the custodian of the House, he had directed the assembly secretariat to obtain information about any member of the KP Assembly, minister, adviser, special assistant to the chief minister or parliamentary secretary who had been arrested or detained. He also sought details of the residences of lawmakers that had been raided, attacked, searched or subjected to similar action by any law enforcement agency. Mr Swati sought a complete report and copies of FIRs concerning such incidents, including those listed in the enclosed list, that had occurred during the last two weeks. According to the letter, the report should be submitted to the assembly secretariat along with records of complaints lodged regarding such incidents at the relevant police stations. Published in Dawn, September 28th, 2026

items.title: Gilgit-Baltistan Scouts soldier, 2 cops injured in Chilas shooting
items.description: GILGIT: A Gilgit-Baltistan Scouts (GBS) soldier and two police personnel were injured in a gun attack on their vehicle near Sher Nallah at Karakoram Highway (KKH) Bash­idas Zero Point in the Chilas area of Diamer district late Sunday evening. GBS is a federal paramilitary force responsible for security, border protection and supporting civil administration across the region. According to a statement issued by the chief minister secretariat, a patrol vehicle of the 116 GBS wing came under fire from the mountain side near Sher Nallah. A GBS soldier and two SSU policemen, who sustained injuries in the attack, were rushed to the Bashidas FWO Hospital where they were given medical treatment before being referred to the RHQ Hospital in Chilas. CM orders investigation, arrest Seeking investigation report of the shooting, Chief Minister Amjad Hussain directed the police and other law enforcement agencies to immediately track down and arrest attackers, planners, and facilitators using all available resources. Stating that attacks on security personnel challenge state authority and would not be tolerated, he ordered strengthened security, surveillance, and search operations in Bashidas, Sher Nallah, and surrounding areas. He also instructed the Diamer authorities to ensure provision of the best medical care to them. No group or individual claimed responsibility for the attack. Published in Dawn, September 28th, 2026

items.title: I resigned five months ago – BoG Governor Asiama explains GoldBod Board exit
items.description: Bank of Ghana (BoG) Governor Dr Johnson Asiama says he resigned from the Board of Directors of the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) about five months ago and no longer participates in its meetings. Dr Asiama said the Ghana Gold Board Act, 2025 (Act 1140), does not require the Bank of Ghana Governor personally to serve on the GoldBod Board. His comments follow concerns raised by the New Patriotic Party (NPP) over his membership of the GoldBod Board and whether his dual roles could create a conflict of interest. Former Finance Minister and NPP MP for Karaga, Dr Mohammed Amin Adam, raised the issue during an NPP press briefing on September 1. The concerns focused on the relationship between the central bank and GoldBod, including the Bank of Ghana’s involvement in financing GoldBod’s gold-purchasing operations and reported losses associated with the domestic gold purchase programme. Dr Asiama, however, said he had already stepped down from the board. “I resigned from the GoldBod Board about five months ago or so. I do not attend board meetings at the GoldBod at all,” Dr Asiama told journalists. He explained that although the law provides for the Bank of Ghana to have representation on the GoldBod Board, the representative need not be the Governor. According to Dr Asiama, the legislation allows either the Governor or another Bank of Ghana official of the required rank to represent the central bank. “The law that governs the activities of the GoldBod, there’s a provision there for the Bank of Ghana to be represented either by the Governor or any other official up to the rank of a director,” he said. He stressed that his personal presence on the board is therefore not a statutory requirement. “It does not necessarily need the Governor to be there.” The explanation comes amid broader scrutiny of the relationship between GoldBod and the central bank, particularly regarding the financing of gold purchases under the domestic gold purchase programme. Dr Asiama’s comments indicate that while the Bank of Ghana is required to have representation on the GoldBod Board, the responsibility can be assigned to another official rather than the Governor.

items.title: Time to fight
items.description: IN my life I have watched communities, organisations, and entire countries lose their grip on truth. I was just starting my book publishing career in Yugoslavia in the mid-80s when the shared facts that held our society together for 40 years came apart, piece by piece, until people could no longer agree on what our country stood for, on its basic values and, finally, what was actually happening. Hundreds of thousands event­ually died. Millions were displaced. Individual lives were ruined. Commu­nities were left devastated, with shards of inhumanity and hurt that were bound to self-regenerate for generations. Decades later, in South Africa, I was part of the opposite movement: a group of dogged journalists digging through the wreckage of state capture, one document at a time, until the theft could no longer be denied. That fundamental work was the very spark that helped pull the country back into hope and, ever so briefly, even optimism. Those two experiences taught me the same lesson from opposite directions. A society that loses its grip on facts loses its grip on itself. A society that fights for truth can still find its way back. That is what World News Day stands for, and why on Sept 28 more than a thousand newsrooms from over a hundred countries will mark it together. World News Day exists so we can strongly express our belief that reliable information is the infrastructure of our modern, information-based society. Like water or electricity, it is fundamental to our existence and yet nobody thinks about it until it isn’t there, or it’s been replaced by something that looks like news but isn’t. Sharing the medium with propaganda outfits and disinformation trolls is one of the great structural weak poi­nts of our entire edifice. Our reports, analyses and investigations travel along the same distribution channels as some of the worst perpetrators of hatred and madness ever to see the face of the Earth. And yet, and yet, we persist. We are still here, because it is our mission, our motivating force, to be on your side no matter what. We will always help you know the facts. They don’t arrive on their own. We have to go and get the facts: read the document, find the witness, check the claims twice, protect sources (who are the ones taking a real risk), ask the questions the powerful people don’t want asked, and then ask them again when they dodge them. We are here to put our name on what we publish and correct it in public if we get it wrong. Algorithmic speed is not the same as truth, and neither is confidence. We will make sure you understand what matters. A data point on its own only tells you that something happened. A flood level, a budget line, a vote count. Journalism’s job is to explain why something happened, who benefited, who paid, and what is likely to come next. The context is often the difference between information and journalism. Information can fill any number of feeds at blinding speed. Journalism has to make sense of the world. It is crucial to choose trusted journalism. This is not a request to trust every newsroom, or to stop asking hard questions of us. Trust is earned over a lifetime, and it has to be re-energised with every new story. I told my guys at Daily Maverick way too many times that we’re only as good as our latest story. But we invite you, the reader, to look out for reporting that shows where its information came from, that separates news from opinion, that admits when it doesn’t know something yet, and that corrects itself when it’s wrong. A trustworthy newsroom isn’t one that never makes mistakes. It’s one you can watch making them right. We owe you the same standard we’re asking you to apply. So on this 2026 World News Day, we’re not just going to tell you that our journalism matters. We’re going to show you and tell you about the work: the months behind an investigation, the checking behind a breaking story, the correction that made the record more accurate, the local report that actually changed the lived reality of a community. Alone, any one of us can be dismissed. In many countries we’re being sued into silence, driven into penury or simply ignored. Still, together, in dozens of languages and more than a hundred countries, we’re harder to ignore. That’s the whole point of doing this on the same day. This is not a fundraiser. This is a rallying point. And here is the fourth thing, the one that drives it all: it’s your right to know. Not a favour handed down by a government or a company that decides what you’re allowed to see. It is your true birth right. World News Day falls on September 28 for a reason: it’s also the UN’s International Day for Universal Access to Information. That’s not a coincidence we’re borrowing for effect. It’s the same idea, seen from two end points. Your right to know is only real if someone is doing the work of making information easy to find, check and, above all, true. That’s the job. So before you share something juicy, pause. Before you believe something, ask how the person telling you knows it. Support the reporting that does this work in the open, and push back on the kind that doesn’t. These have never mattered more: Know the facts. Understand what matters. Choose trusted journalism. Because it’s your right to know. And because a world that stops knowing will never be free — just easier to fool. See you in the trenches. The writer is the founder of Project Kontinuum, an alliance of people working to return journalism to its role as an essential service. This opinion piece was commissioned as part of the World News Day campaign highlighting the essential role of journalism in providing facts and clarity. Published in Dawn, September 28th, 2026

items.title: PML-N claims victory in Bahawalpur by-poll
items.description: BAHAWALPUR: PML-N candidate Malik Munir Iqbal Channar was leading independent candidate Wali Dad Cheema in the NA-168 (Bahawalpur-V) by-election at most of the 292 polling stations until late Sunday, according to unofficial results. Mr Channar had secured 62,713 votes against Mr Cheema’s 31,293, suggesting that the ruling party was set to retain the National Assembly seat that fell vacant following the death of MNA Malik Muhammad Iqbal Channar. The PML-N had fielded the deceased MNA’s son to contest the by-election. The polling process was largely peaceful across the constituency, although there were reports of isolated incidents of violence, mismanagement, confusion and complaints about the unavailability of women’s voter lists at some polling stations. Unofficial tally suggests Channar has secured nearly double the votes of his main rival, Cheema In a statement, the provincial election commissioner said balloting was briefly disrupted at a polling station in Akhtarabad, considered a PML-N stronghold, following a brawl between voters after political workers allegedly harassed election staff. Immediate action was taken, and the relevant district returning officer and returning officer brought the situation under control with police help. Polling remained slow during the early hours, with limited voter participation. Although polling began on time at all stations on Sunday morning, staff remained idle for several hours as only a few voters turned up till noon. However, voter turnout, including among women, increased after midday. Rural polling stations, particularly those around Jhnagiwali and Abbasnagar, which are considered strongholds of the Channar family, witnessed a large number of voters. When asked about the incident, Mr Channar alleged that some people had disrupted polling and were found stamping ballot papers in favour of his rival. He claimed that the individuals were expelled following the scuffle and that polling resumed after remaining suspended for several hours. Meanwhile, some voters at the Bahawalpur 3-Marla Housing Scheme polling station alleged police officials deployed there had not allowed voters whose CNICs carried addresses from the Yazman area, which is considered a stronghold of Mr Cheema, to cast their ballots. PM congratulates party candidate Later, a statement issued by PM Office said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif congratulated Malik Munir Iqbal Channar as well as his brother Malik Zaheer Iqbal Channar, who is incumbent Punjab Assembly deputy speaker, on the victory in the by-election. The PM lauded the people of Bahawalpur for electing their representative, stating that the victory showed public confidence in the PML-N.
